result: The Frh complex from M. marburgensis is a 1.2-MDa dodecamer with tetrahedral symmetry, forming a spherical protein shell with a hollow core rather than the previously proposed cylindrical arrangement. This structure was determined by cryo-EM at near-atomic resolution using 84,000 particles.
evaluation: Claims C4, C27, C6-C7, C30-C36 collectively establish the quaternary structure of Frh through cryo-EM analysis. The tetrahedral symmetry is supported by class averages showing twofold and threefold symmetry (C31), the spherical arrangement is visible in the 3D reconstruction (C36), and the dodecameric composition is calculated from the heterotrimer stoichiometry (C32-C33). The resolution quality is demonstrated by visible α-helical pitch and separated β-strands (C34), and the lack of preferred orientation is shown by homogeneous Euler angle coverage (C35). This contradicts previous negative stain EM interpretations (C23) and represents a major structural finding.

result: Each FrhABG heterotrimer contains a complete electron transfer chain with five metal centers ([NiFe] cluster and four Fe-S clusters) arranged in a curvilinear path with ~10 Å spacing between neighbors, running from the [NiFe] center through Fe-S clusters to FAD.
evaluation: Claims C8, C37-C38, C88-C89 describe the electron transfer pathway based on high-density features visible in the cryo-EM map. The five metal centers are clearly resolved and assigned based on size differences (C37-C38), their spatial arrangement is documented (C89), and the functional electron transfer chain is traced through all three subunits (C88). The ~10 Å spacing is appropriate for electron transfer, and the arrangement is consistent across all 12 heterotrimers in the complex.

result: The F420-binding site is located near the outside of the spherical structure, in van der Waals contact with the FAD isoalloxazine ring, as determined by difference mapping between substrate-free and F420-bound structures.
evaluation: Claims C9, C90, C120-C121 establish the F420 binding site location through difference mapping. The position was initially identified by comparing maps with and without substrate (C120), then confirmed by model building showing F420 in van der Waals contact with FAD (C121) and surrounded by highly conserved residues (C121). The external location facilitates substrate access (C90). While the F420 density is weak, the consistent difference between substrate-free and substrate-bound maps, combined with the structural and sequence conservation evidence, supports this assignment.

result: FrhB was traced de novo from the cryo-EM map and has a novel fold with no structural homologs, using secondary structure predictions, Fe-S cluster ligand positions, and visible side chain densities to guide model building.
evaluation: Claims C5, C68-C69, C74, C122-C125 describe the de novo structure determination of FrhB. The absence of structural homologs is established by database searches (C68, C71, C73), necessitating ab initio modeling (C69). The model building strategy using Fe-S cluster cysteines, secondary structure predictions, and side chain densities is well-documented (C122-C123), and the correctness is validated by full confirmation of secondary structure predictions (C124) and correlation of weak densities with glycine positions (C125). This represents a significant structural achievement.

result: FrhA shows considerable structural homology to group 1 [NiFe]-hydrogenase large subunits, with conserved core elements including the four-helix bundle and [NiFe] center coordination, but is ~15 kDa smaller with peripheral elements missing.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45, C47, C49 establish FrhA structure through homology modeling. The structural similarity to group 1 hydrogenases is demonstrated by good fit of the homologous structure (C42), with conserved elements including the α-helix bundle, β-sheets, and [NiFe] center coordination by four cysteines (C45). The size difference is explained by missing peripheral elements (C43). Model quality is supported by nearly complete tracing (C44) and specific features like the proline-induced helix kink (C49). The presence of an additional conserved ion (C47) further validates the model.

result: FrhG consists of an N-terminal domain with structural homology to group 1 hydrogenase small subunits (containing the proximal Fe-S cluster with unusual Asp60 coordination) and a C-terminal ferredoxin domain with two additional Fe-S clusters.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55, C57-C60, C62 describe FrhG structure through a combination of homology modeling and sequence analysis. The N-terminal domain homology is established by structural fit (C53-C55), with the unusual aspartate ligand for the proximal Fe-S cluster supported by precedent (C58). The C-terminal ferredoxin domain is identified by sequence motifs (C60) and modeled accordingly, with the β-hairpin visible in density confirming the assignment (C62). The lower overall similarity compared to FrhA (C54) is acknowledged.

result: FrhB contains a [4Fe4S] cluster coordinated by four conserved cysteines and an FAD cofactor in a bent conformation, with the pyrophosphate positioned at an N-terminal helix dipole in a common FAD-binding motif, surrounded by highly conserved residues.
evaluation: Claims C75, C77-C80, C126-C130 describe the cofactor binding in FrhB. The [4Fe4S] cluster assignment is based on four cysteine ligands and sequence conservation (C75). The FAD is identified by density ~8 Å from the Fe-S cluster (C77), with the pyrophosphate at a helix N-terminus representing a known FAD-binding motif (C78-C79, C129). The bent FAD conformation (C79) and surrounding conserved residues (C80, C130) support the model. Missing density for ribose and ribitol (C127) is acknowledged but does not undermine the overall assignment.

result: FrhA undergoes C-terminal proteolytic processing after His386, likely by the homologous endopeptidase FrhD encoded in the same operon, similar to maturation of other [NiFe]-hydrogenases.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 establish post-translational modification of FrhA. The absence of density beyond His386 (C50) is consistent with known proteolytic processing of [NiFe]-hydrogenases (C51). The inference that FrhD performs this processing (C52) is reasonable given its presence in the operon and homology to known hydrogenase proteases, though direct experimental evidence is not provided. This represents a well-supported inference based on structural and genomic data.

result: The frhG gene likely starts at GTG (Val39 in the genome annotation) rather than the annotated start codon, based on the absence of density for the first 45 amino acids of the genome-predicted sequence.
evaluation: Claims C65-C66 propose a corrected start codon for frhG. The absence of density for 45 N-terminal residues (C65) combined with precedent for GTG as an alternative start codon (C66) supports this reassignment. This reduces the missing residues to only seven, which is more consistent with the otherwise complete models of FrhA and FrhB. The inference is well-supported by both structural and literature evidence.

result: The functional unit is a single FrhABG heterotrimer with no cooperativity between heterotrimers, as electron transfer chains in dimers are separated by at least 17 Å.
evaluation: Claims C91-C92 establish the functional independence of heterotrimers based on distance measurements. The 17 Å separation between electron transfer chains in a dimer (C91) is too large for efficient electron transfer, supporting the conclusion of independent functional units (C92). This is a reasonable inference from the structural data, though functional studies would provide additional support.

result: The FrhABG heterotrimer forms a tight complex with extensive subunit interfaces including salt bridges between FrhA molecules in dimers, though the heterotrimer is slender compared to two-subunit [NiFe]-hydrogenases, suggesting complex formation is necessary for stability.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 describe intersubunit interactions. Specific salt bridges are identified (C93), and the slender nature of the heterotrimer is documented by comparison (C94). The speculation about stability (C95) is reasonable but not directly tested. The structural observations are well-supported, though the functional interpretation remains speculative.

result: The dodecameric quaternary structure is conserved across phylogenetically diverse methanogenic archaea (M. thermautotrophicus, M. voltae, M. hungatei), indicating it plays an essential role in Frh function.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 establish functional importance through evolutionary conservation. The observation of similar quaternary structure across diverse species (C96) supports the inference of functional importance (C97). However, the previous EM studies cited interpreted the structure as cylindrical rather than spherical, so the conservation refers to overall size and appearance rather than the specific dodecameric spherical arrangement now revealed.

result: The cryo-EM reconstruction resolution is estimated at 3.9-4.0 Å by conventional FSC (0.5 criterion), 5.5 Å by gold-standard FSC (0.143 criterion), with local resolution ~4.5 Å in well-resolved regions based on visible α-helical pitch and β-strand separation, and 5.8 Å model-to-map FSC.
evaluation: Claims C104-C114 provide multiple resolution estimates using different criteria. The conventional FSC gives 3.9-4.0 Å (C104), but this is acknowledged to potentially overestimate resolution due to noise correlation (C105). The gold-standard procedure gives 5.5 Å (C106), while visual inspection of secondary structure suggests ~4.5 Å locally (C107-C109). The model-to-map FSC of 5.8 Å (C111) reflects both map quality and model completeness (C112-C113). The use of tight restraints during modeling (C114) appropriately prevents overfitting. The multiple complementary approaches provide a thorough resolution assessment.

result: Several factors contributed to successful high-resolution structure determination: tetrahedral symmetry providing 12 asymmetric units, ball-like shape preventing preferred orientation, complex rigidity, and minimal conformational changes upon F420 binding.
evaluation: Claims C115-C119 analyze factors contributing to the successful structure determination. The tetrahedral symmetry (C116), lack of preferred orientation (C117), rigidity (C118), and minimal substrate-induced changes (C119) are all supported by the data. These represent reasonable interpretations of why high resolution was achieved, though some factors (like rigidity) are inferred from the quality of the reconstruction rather than directly measured.

result: FrhB shares conserved cofactor-coordinating residues and a common fold with a family of F420-dependent enzymes including sulfite reductase, quinone oxidoreductase, phenazine oxidoreductase, glutamate synthase, and formate dehydrogenase.
evaluation: Claims C132-C134 establish the FrhB protein family through sequence conservation. The conservation of Fe-S cluster, FAD, and F420-coordinating residues across diverse F420-dependent enzymes (C132) supports the inference of a common fold (C134). The presence of additional domains in some family members (C133) is noted. This represents a well-supported bioinformatic analysis extending the structural findings.

result: All three protein models follow expected principles of protein structure with hydrophobic cores and charged surfaces, including hydrophobic pockets and a buried hydrophobic helix in FrhB, indicating correct chain tracing.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 provide validation of model quality through general structural principles. The observation that all three proteins follow hydrophobic core/charged surface rules (C84), contain hydrophobic pockets (C85), and include a buried hydrophobic helix in FrhB (C86) supports model correctness (C87). These are appropriate quality checks for protein structure models.

result: FrhG has missing density for residues 188-199, which likely form a flexible surface loop based on the proximity of flanking residues (<10 Å apart).
evaluation: Claims C63-C64, C81-C82 describe a disordered region in FrhG. The missing density (C63, C81) and surface location (C64) support the interpretation of a flexible loop (C82), with the proximity of flanking residues (C82) indicating the region is not large. This is a reasonable interpretation of incomplete density in an otherwise well-resolved structure.

result: The final cryo-EM datasets contained 84,000 particles (substrate-free) and 97,000 particles (F420-bound) with B-factors of 54 Å² and 60 Å² respectively.
evaluation: Claims C138-C140 report dataset statistics. These are straightforward data reporting claims that describe the number of particles used and the estimated B-factors. The values are consistent with high-quality cryo-EM reconstructions.

result: The final model contains 878 of 903 possible residues plus all cofactors, with 88.1% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions, 8.0% in allowed regions, and 3.8% outliers.
evaluation: Claims C141-C142 report model completeness and stereochemical quality. The high percentage of modeled residues (97.2%) and favorable Ramachandran statistics indicate good model quality, though the 3.8% outliers is somewhat high for a structure at this resolution. This likely reflects the challenges of modeling at ~4-5 Å resolution and the use of tight restraints to prevent overfitting.
